topics.label: Introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and sets out what students should learn about cancer causation.

topics.label: Mutations and the conditions for cancer development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how mutations arise and enable clonal evolution when the affected cells and their microenvironment permit cancer development.

topics.label: Environmental contributions to cancer risk
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how far environmental exposures explain cancer risk rather than inherited susceptibility or chance.

topics.label: Infectious agents in cancer development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections can drive cancer, using Burkitt lymphoma to develop the interaction between pathogens and malignant transformation.

topics.label: Mechanisms of exposure-induced DNA damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental carcinogens produce DNA damage that can become mutations, with their activity often depending on metabolism.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish mutational initiation from the promotion of tumour growth and explain why an initiating mutation alone may be insufficient.

topics.label: Tissue and developmental context of carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show that carcinogenic effects depend on the biological context of exposure and consolidate that principle within the preceding account of cancer causation.

topics.label: Assessing carcinogenicity and attributing cancer to exposures
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how evidence can establish an exposure's carcinogenic potential or contribution to cancer while accounting for the limitations of the available methods.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing draws together the lecture's conclusions about environmental cancer risks and the difficulty of assessing them to frame everyday risk–benefit decisions.
